title: Adab of travel
hook: a verse for setting off, company on the road, and praise on the way home

segments.voice: Yesterday, the adab of guests, and your line: honor the guest. Today the courtesy leaves the house with you.

The seatbelt clicks. The engine turns over. And before the car pulls out, the driver says a line under her breath, in Arabic. It isn't a line about cars. It comes from the Qur'an, from a passage about riding animals and ships, written long before any engine. Partway through, it admits something. It ends by mentioning a destination that isn't on any map in the car. Today: the manners of leaving home, and of coming back.
screen: `THE SEATBELT CLICKS.` → `A LINE BEFORE PULLING OUT.` → `A DESTINATION NOT ON THE MAP.`

segments.voice: Ibn 'Umar describes it in Sahih Muslim. When the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, mounted his camel to set out on a journey, he said Allahu akbar three times, then recited two verses of al-Zukhruf. In Pickthall's translation: "Glorified be He Who hath subdued these unto us, and we were not capable (of subduing them); And lo! unto our Lord we surely are returning." The admission first: we were not capable. The animal, the ship, today the car or the plane: none of it is ours by our own strength. Then the turn: unto our Lord we are returning. Every trip has a return built in, and the verse points past it to the last return of all. In the same report, he asked for goodness on the journey and for the distance to be made easy. Coming home, he said it again and added: returning, repenting, worshipping, praising our Lord. Two more pieces. Company: a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says, in paraphrase, that if people knew what he knew about traveling alone, no rider would travel alone at night. And home: another hadith in Bukhari calls travel a piece of torment, because it keeps a person from food, drink and sleep, so when your business is done, hurry back to your family. Leave remembering. Travel with others where you can. Come home quickly, praising.
screen: `WE WERE NOT CAPABLE OF IT.` · `UNTO OUR LORD WE ARE RETURNING.` · `NOT ALONE AT NIGHT.` · `DONE? HURRY HOME, PRAISING.`

segments.voice: Picture the next trip you'll take, even across town, and see yourself sitting down in the seat. If you pray, you can say the words now, in Arabic if you know them, or in English: Glorified be He Who hath subdued these unto us; if you don't, just notice how much of the trip you didn't build, the road, the engine, the hands that made them. Then see yourself walking back through your own door, and stay with that return.
Adab of travel. The manners of the road: remember Allah setting out, keep company where you can, and come home quickly, praising. Today's word.
Your line: travel remembering. Every trip has a return built in. That's day one thousand two hundred ninety-six.

howItsDone: Muslims setting out on a journey say Allahu akbar and recite the verses of al-Zukhruf, "Glorified be He Who hath subdued these unto us," in Arabic, and on returning add words of praise.

original.note: Arabic: journey, travel; a traveler is a musafir.

trapdoor: what you thought: the travel du'a is a prayer for a safe trip.
what it means: a verse that admits we didn't tame the ride ourselves, and remembers that every road ends in a return to our Lord.
what a scholar hears: Ibn 'Umar's report in Sahih Muslim: three takbirs, al-Zukhruf 43:13–14, and on the way back, returning, repenting, worshipping, praising.

chat.says: Why do some Muslims say a prayer before the car even starts?
options: It's the travel du'a: we weren't capable of this ourselves, and to our Lord we return.
It's a charm against accidents; the words are meant to guarantee a safe trip.
It's only for long journeys by camel; it was never meant for cars.
chat.meaning: Setting out, the Prophet recited from al-Zukhruf: glorified be He who subdued these for us, we weren't capable, and to our Lord we return.

al-Zukhruf.meaning: a surah of the Qur'an, The Ornaments of Gold

Ibn 'Umar.meaning: Abdullah, son of Umar, a companion who reported this
